issues.legal_issue: A delegated rule may reserve the exclusive right to quarry a minor mineral to the State and prohibit private quarrying where that measure is within the State’s regulatory authority and serves a public-interest purpose.
material_facts: A committee reported extensive environmental and structural damage caused by haphazard, unscientific and unauthorized private sand quarrying.
The committee recommended prohibiting private quarrying, and the State decided to undertake sand quarrying exclusively.
issues.conclusion: The provision vesting the exclusive right to quarry sand in the State was valid.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 empowers the State to make rules regulating quarry leases for minor minerals. The regulatory power can extend to prohibiting private exploitation and reserving exploitation to the State in an appropriate case. State of Tamil Nadu v. Hind Stone and Gem Granites v. State of Tamil Nadu recognize that power.

predicates.challenge_to_delegated_mining_rule: The proceeding challenges a rule made under delegated authority to regulate mining or quarrying.
predicates.expert_committee_found_environmental_har: An expert committee found that private quarrying caused environmental or related public harm.
predicates.state_adopted_exclusive_quarrying_policy: The State adopted a policy of undertaking quarrying exclusively to address that harm and serve the public interest.

issues.definition: When a delegated mining rule is challenged, an expert committee has found environmental harm from private quarrying, and the State adopted an exclusive-quarrying policy for the public interest, the State’s exclusive quarrying right is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A delegated rule cannot immediately terminate subsisting mining leases contrary to the governing law’s protection of lease rights and requirement of a hearing, but it may be read down to operate through the lease’s termination-notice provision.
material_facts: Private holders had leases that were subsisting when the rule took effect, and the rule purported to terminate them immediately.
The governing Act provided for a holder’s opportunity to be heard before premature termination of a mining lease.
The leases contained a term allowing either side to terminate on six months’ notice, and the State had decided to end private quarrying.
issues.conclusion: The immediate termination of subsisting leases was not valid as written. The rule was read down to terminate such leases on six months’ notice or the shorter unexpired lease period, whichever was less. A lease could instead be terminated earlier on statutory grounds after notice and a hearing. Affected holders were entitled to quarry during the applicable period, subject to lawful earlier termination.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4A(2) and 4A(3) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 provide for premature termination on specified grounds and require a reasonable opportunity of hearing; section 24A recognizes the rights of a leaseholder during the lease. A delegated rule cannot contradict the parent Act’s scheme. Although legislative rule-making ordinarily does not require observance of natural justice, an enabling Act may expressly require a hearing. State of Haryana v. Ram Kishan treats lease termination under section 4A as executive action; Rameshchandra Kachardas Porwal and Union of India v. Cynamide India Ltd. address natural justice in legislative activity; Shri Sitaram Sugar Co. Ltd. v. Union of India addresses the limits on delegated power. The offending provision may be saved by reading it down where a valid, severable construction is available.

predicates.challenge_to_delegated_mining_rule: The proceeding challenges a rule made under delegated authority to regulate mining or quarrying.
predicates.subsisting_mining_lease_at_rule_commence: A person held a mining lease that remained in force when the rule took effect.
predicates.governing_law_protects_lease_rights_and_: The governing law protects operations under a subsisting lease and requires a hearing before its premature termination.
predicates.lease_allows_termination_on_notice: The lease terms allow either side to terminate the lease by giving notice.

issues.definition: If a challenged delegated mining rule affects a subsisting lease protected by the governing law, and the lease allows termination on notice, the lease ends only after the contractual notice period or the shorter unexpired term unless it is earlier terminated after a hearing on lawful grounds.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory hearing requirement for premature termination of a mining lease does not prevent the immediate cessation of quarrying by a person whose authority is only a permit or who has no subsisting mining lease.
material_facts: The rule directed that existing sand-quarrying permissions cease when it took effect.
Some people quarrying sand were not acting under subsisting mining leases.
The statutory hearing requirement addressed premature termination of mining leases.
issues.conclusion: Quarrying permissions ceased when the rule took effect, as did quarrying by persons without subsisting mining leases; no hearing was required before that cessation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4A(3) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 requires a hearing before premature termination of a mining lease. That requirement applies to holders of subsisting mining leases, not to permit holders or persons quarrying without such a lease.

predicates.challenge_to_delegated_mining_rule: The proceeding challenges a rule made under delegated authority to regulate mining or quarrying.
predicates.quarrying_authority_was_only_a_permit_or: The person’s authority to quarry consisted only of a permit, or the person had no subsisting mining lease.

issues.definition: When a challenged delegated mining rule concerns a person whose quarrying authority was only a permit or no subsisting lease, that authority ceases without a prior hearing.
